title: Needle
background: The Thread is the editorial style and visual design magazine of RPI, celebrating fashion and design culture across Troy. The organization needed a digital home for editorial content, event programming, and community contributions—and a secure workspace for officers to manage it all.

Needle is the web-suite built to answer that: public-facing storytelling and internal operations in one platform for viewers, contributors, and authorized members. Developed with a five-person team across design, frontend, and backend.

backgroundImages.alt: The signature mark of The Thread.

process: The Needle web-suite runs on React, Flask, and MongoDB Atlas with AWS S3. API design followed a frontend-first approach, iterating from page-driven routes toward a consolidated events–images–members model.

The Thread anchors every public page as header and footer, setting the design language for the site. Event discovery centers on a card system—several landing layouts, including a Loop component for recent programming, were explored before the team settled on what shipped. Admin breaks deliberately from that aesthetic: The Thread doesn't appear in the workspace, and the visual language shifts sharper and more utilitarian for club officers on the same data.

processImages.alt: Needle data architecture evolution: dataflow draft, schema v2, and proposed entity model
Needle imageDB schema: S3 asset paths, event references, and personnel attribution
Early Figma mockup: The Thread as a winding path with ribbon header navigation and a mixed-scale event card grid
Early landing sketches: Fits of the Week gallery and UPCOMING timeline along The Thread — concepts explored before the shipped event card system
Early Figma mockup: The Loop — a vertical recent-programming stack on the landing hero, explored then cut
Early event card explorations at hero, editorial, and thumbnail scales, with type labels and iconography
Event detail explorations: mobile-first layouts and tablet iconography iterations
Early rounded admin exploration: edit event form with soft corners, type icons, personnel, and image management
Admin portal: Figma exploration vs. shipped login and events management views

result: Needle ships an efficient fullstack dataflow, visually aligned as the digital base of The Thread.
The public interface embodies The Thread’s mission: The Thread itself stitches every page together through soft type and rounded forms—unorthodox and playful, yet systematic.
Published past events—with detailed views, associated images, and members—are live, and the groundwork for a semesterly calendar, member profiles, and PDF publications is laid for future development.

Behind auth, the admin workspace keeps a related but sharper identity: explicitly defined rectangular regions with thin black strokes, resembling a management dashboard yet clearly part of The Thread brand—and a near-complete custom CMS gives officers full data visualization and the infrastructure to manage that same data, with role-based permissions in place.

title: Historical Archive of Black Design
background: The Mius Thomas Historical Archive of Black Design (Archive, for short) is my vision for a central digital system that stores, maps, and organizes the earliest contributions of African American/Soulaani people to graphic arts and design, and ultimately serves as their source of truth.

Archive needs to exist because the accepted design canon, like those of many other arts and industries, rarely acknowledges the contributions of African American/Soulaani people, groups, and culture. Shaped by centuries of political, economic, and social forces, it is fundamentally incapable of doing so. Many excellent Black archives preserve artifacts and histories that their generalized peers neglect, but there is no dedicated source of truth for Black design. As a Black design scholar who struggled to find the work of my predecessors, I learned the hard way that we have always been, and will continue to be, overlooked by the mainstream canon. So I set out to make sure future Black designers never struggle to see themselves in the discipline they love.

It started with a question I asked in my Fall 2025 Typography course that I still can’t answer: “Who was the first Black (graphic) designer?” That personal research became an independent study under Dr. Adam Biggs in Spring 2026, culminating in a research paper and a UX prototype that brings my vision to life.

backgroundImages.alt: Entry assets for Archive UI exploration
Excerpt from the independent study research paper behind Archive

process: Archive’s visual language extends that of my personal brand: colorless and predominantly black to carry the weight of the work, minimal and sharp so the catalog holds the user’s focus. Every entry, whether a person, movement, organization, or work, is essential to this narrative yet overlooked in most others, so the interface acts as the stage they were never given.

Entries began as individuals while I searched for the first Black designers, but the criteria slowly grew to include organizations, movements, mediums, and the works they produced, telling a more complete story than a single question could. I defined a data model for each collection to standardize similar entries. That let me design one reusable collection interface and a reusable entry interface per model, cutting my design overhead. I gave up tailoring interfaces to individual entries, but for an archive meant to catalog and spotlight a near-endless body of overlooked work, the consistency and speed are well worth it.

The reusable collection interface was designed in a rush. It lacked key design heuristics, like collection iconography, and archival functionality, like embedded search and filtering to narrow down entries. I revised the screen to add those motifs and features, making the collection view more visually aligned with the system and more capable as an archive.

processImages.alt: Logo exploration for Archive, continued for the full signature logotype

result: The prototype covers mobile views of the landing page with featured entries, global search, the menu, and each collection, plus entry views for Aaron Douglas and the Harlem Renaissance (New Negro Movement). Most collections use the original reusable collection interface, and the Groups and Organizations collection demos the upgraded one.

Archive is still just a vision: a Figma prototype with no codebase or database. Next, I intend to refine a few more of the existing interfaces and create desktop counterparts, before planning implementation, including final entry models, end-to-end data flow, and component architecture.
